QuakeScope · PR #71 · 2026-10-26

Faster PhaseNet: do the picks change?

PR #71 proposes a faster way to run the QuakeScope picker on CPUs, found by an automated optimization tool (VibeSys). We re-picked the leaderboard's waveforms with it and compared every pick.

Answer PR #71 Picker leaderboard

Answer

fp32 keeps every pick. fp16 stays within a 30 ms tolerance; bf16 does not.

PR #71 rewrites how PhaseNet and the amplitude code run on a CPU. We re-picked the leaderboard's 26,531 picks (threshold 0.2, weight PhaseNet original, weight version 2) three ways and compared each pick with the current code's.

fp32 · what the PR uses on Fargate and Graviton

26,529 of 26,531

picks identical to the millisecond

The other 2 moved by one sample (10 ms) on a flat-topped peak. Amplitudes agree to 9e-12. Runs 5.9 to 6.6 times faster on Graviton.

fp16 · not in the PR, tested for comparison

98.7 %

picks identical

99.83 % within 30 ms; 29 picks move further (up to 420 ms). Picks gained or lost all sit at the threshold. Speed not measured.

bf16 · the PR's mode on Intel AMX CPUs only

89.3 %

picks identical

98.06 % within 30 ms; 333 picks move further (up to 480 ms) and 437 appear or disappear. No speed gain on our hardware, which has no AMX.

Against the 7,593 analyst picks, none of the three changes recall by more than 0.001 or mean absolute error by more than 1 ms, and none moves the median bias. The difference is in reproducing the catalogue, not in accuracy.

Background

What fp32, fp16 and bf16 are

They are ways of storing each number inside the network. Fewer bits make the arithmetic faster on CPUs built for it, and round every intermediate value more coarsely. Think of it as digitizer resolution applied to every layer of PhaseNet.

formatbits per valuebits of precisionrounding step (relative)largest value
fp32 (single precision)3224, like a 24-bit digitizer6×10-83×1038
fp16 (half precision)16115×10-465,504
bf16 ("brain float")1684×10-33×1038

PhaseNet's output is a probability trace per phase, and a pick is the sample where it peaks above the threshold. Rounding perturbs that trace a little. Where the peak is sharp nothing happens; where it is flat the maximum can jump to a neighbouring sample, and where it sits near the threshold the pick can appear or disappear. Under bf16 the 99th percentile change in the trace's peak value is 0.045; under fp32 it is too small to measure at the 10-4 level.

Your tolerance

Choose what counts as the same pick

Starts at a 30 ms tolerance with 0.5 % of picks allowed to fail; change either. Picks that appear or disappear only because they sit just at the threshold are excused by the confidence margin.

A pick fails when it moves by more than the tolerance, or when it is lost or new and its confidence is more than the margin above the threshold. Per-pick data: errors_pr_fp32.csv.gz · errors_pr_fp16.csv.gz · errors_pr_bf16.csv.gz.

Speed

Six times faster on AWS Graviton, in fp32

The same 5.55 station-days (42 benchmark windows) processed by four workers on an 8-vCPU machine, the shape of a Fargate task. Median of four repetitions; picking and amplitudes included, S3 reads and writes not.

machinecurrent codePR, fp32fasterSpot $ per 1,000 station-days
M1 Max laptop150 s129 s1.2×–
c6g.2xlarge (Graviton2)145 s22 s6.6×$0.58 → $0.09
c7g.2xlarge (Graviton3)93 s16 s5.9×$0.38 → $0.06
c8g.2xlarge (Graviton4)77 s13 s6.1×$0.30 → $0.05

Where the time goes

Most of the saving is the Wood-Anderson amplitude code: 90 % of the time saved on Graviton4. PhaseNet itself runs 1.7× faster there. These windows are aftershock sequences with many picks; an ordinary station-day has far fewer, so the gain in a campaign will be smaller. Not yet measured.

Why the laptop gains little

The PR's fast PhaseNet needs a library (oneDNN) that no macOS build of PyTorch includes, so on an Apple laptop only the amplitude code speeds up, and picking runs 1.34× slower.

Prices: on-demand from the AWS Pricing API, cheapest-AZ Spot from describe_spot_price_history, both 2026-10-26. For comparison, Fargate Spot costs about $0.17/h for the same 8 vCPU (CloudBank billing). Fargate itself was not timed.

Details

Method, full tables, limits

What each mode runs

Current code: sbm.PhaseNet.from_pretrained("original").classify and main's AmplitudeExtractor() at 7dd1be7. fp32: PR head a5d4d43 with the settings of its removed runner (vibesys/pick_workload.py at 4271d67): BatchNorm folded into the convolutions, polyphase transposed convolutions, fast windowing (glue=fused), amplitudes impl="fused", signal="slim". bf16 and fp16: the same, with weights and inputs in 16 bits, fp32 accumulation, and every layer's output rounded to 16 bits. This emulates Intel AMX for bf16 and is a best case for fp16. Run on the M1 Max laptop.

Precision workload: 130 cached station-windows of docs/benchmark/results/{us,swarm}_sequences, 7,593 analyst picks. Picks at a 0.02 floor, thresholded afterwards, paired with benchmark_metrics.match_picks within 0.5 s. The cached waveforms for Mendocino, Monroe and San Simeon CI are not the streams the leaderboard picked, so absolute US recall differs from the board; every mode read the same files.

Limits and defects found in the PR
  • jma_wc, the global weight, was not scored. obs (PickBlue) cannot use the fast path: building it raises does not cover this model setup: ['padding/filter'].
  • bf16 was emulated, not run on AMX hardware. fp16 speed was not measured.
  • Streams the model resamples (30 of 130 windows) fall back to SeisBench's windowing. Timing used 100 Hz only.
  • The 707-line s3_helper.py rewrite was not reviewed.
  • veliir.c (velocity amplitudes) does not build on ARM, so SciPy ran on Graviton. Built with its x86-only CPU probe guarded, it matched SciPy to 10-11.
  • As merged, nothing selects the fast settings, so production would run the current code.
Reproduce

Harness in scripts/vibesys_pr71/; export_results.py writes the tables in docs/benchmark/results/vibesys_pr71/, and scripts/build_vibesys_report.py builds this page from them.

  2. Zhu, W. and Beroza, G. C. (2019). PhaseNet: a deep-neural-network-based seismic arrival-time picking method. Geophysical Journal International 216, 261-273. doi:10.1093/gji/ggy423
